'''Kenneth Michael Stabler''' (December 25, 1945 – July 8, 2015) was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[quarterback]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 17 seasons, primarily with the [[Oakland Raiders]]. Nicknamed "'''Snake'''", he played [[college football]] for the [[Alabama Crimson Tide football|Alabama Crimson Tide]] and was selected by the Raiders in the second round of the [[1968 NFL/AFL draft]]. During his 10 seasons in Oakland, Stabler received four [[Pro Bowl]] selections and was named [[National Football League Most Valuable Player Award|Most Valuable Player]] in 1974. Stabler also helped the Raiders win their first [[Super Bowl]] title in [[Super Bowl XI]]. He was posthumously inducted to the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2016.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Hoffman |first=Benjamin |date=February 6, 2016 |title=After Revelation He Had C.T.E., Ken Stabler Is a Poignant Hall of Fame Addition |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/02/07/sports/football/ken-stabler-nfl-hall-of-fame.html |work=The New York Times}}</ref>

Head coach | highlights = ;As assistant coach * [[List of Super Bowl champions|Super Bowl champion]] ([[Super Bowl XL|XL]]) * PFWA NFL Assistant Coach of the Year (2013) * First-team [[List of All-Atlantic Coast Conference football teams|All-ACC]] ([[1984 All-Atlantic Coast Conference football team|1984]]) | statlabel1 = [[Reception (gridiron football)|Receptions]] | statvalue1 = 62 | statlabel2 = Receiving yards | statvalue2 = 596 | statlabel3 = Receiving [[touchdown]]s | statvalue3 = 5 | regular_record = {{Winning percentage|48|71|record=y}} | playoff_record = {{Winning percentage|4|2|record=y}} | overall_record = {{Winning percentage|52|73|record=y}} | pfrcoach = WhisKe0 }} '''Kenneth Moore Whisenhunt''' (born February 28, 1962) is an American [[American football|football]] coach and former [[tight end]]. He played college football at [[Georgia Tech]] and was selected in the twelfth round of the [[1985 NFL draft]] by the [[Atlanta Falcons]], with whom he played for four years. Whisenhunt subsequently played two more years with the [[Washington Redskins]] and another two with the [[New York Jets]]. Beginning his coaching career in 1995, Whisenhunt was [[head coach]] of the [[Arizona Cardinals]] from [[2007 Arizona Cardinals season|2007]] to [[2012 Arizona Cardinals season|2012]] and [[Tennessee Titans]] from [[2014 Tennessee Titans season|2014]] to [[2015 Tennessee Titans season|2015]]. He led the Cardinals to their first [[Super Bowl]] appearance in franchise history during the [[2008 NFL season|2008 season]], as well as their first home playoff games in 60 years. However, following the retirement of [[Kurt Warner]], Whisenhunt posted three straight non-winning seasons and was fired by the Cardinals. He was fired by the Titans after compiling a record of 3–20 through {{frac|1|1|2}} years. Overall, Whisenhunt posted a record of 48–71 as head coach, including a 4–31 record in his last 35 games as a head coach. Whisenhunt was 4–2 in the playoffs, but missed them in five of his seven seasons as coach. Among all coaches who have won a conference championship as a coach, Whisenhunt has the lowest winning percentage at .403.{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/coaches/|title=Coaches, Records, and Coaching Totals|website=Pro Football Reference}} Prior to and after his tenures as head coach of the Cardinals and Titans, Whisenhunt served as an offensive coordinator to various NFL teams. He had success with the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] in his three years as their [[offensive coordinator]] under [[Bill Cowher]] and winning [[Super Bowl XL]] over the [[Seattle Seahawks]] during the [[2005 NFL season|2005 season]]. Most recently, Whisenhunt served as the [[offensive coordinator]] for the [[Los Angeles Chargers]] for four seasons before being fired on October 28, 2019.

'''Kenneth Walter''' (born August 15, 1972) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Punter (football)|punter]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played for the [[Carolina Panthers]] from [[1997 NFL season|1997]]–[[2000 NFL season|2000]], the [[New England Patriots]] from [[2001 New England Patriots season|2001]]–[[2003 New England Patriots season|2003]] and [[2006 New England Patriots season|2006]] and the [[Seattle Seahawks]] in [[2004 NFL season|2004]]. He played [[College football|collegiately]] for [[Kent State University]].

On the Patriots, Walter served as the holder for [[placekicker]] [[Adam Vinatieri]].  He successfully held for both of Vinatieri's Super Bowl winning kicks in [[Super Bowl XXXVI]] and [[Super Bowl XXXVIII]]. He also held for Vinatieri's famous kicks in the [[Tuck Rule Game]] against the [[Oakland Raiders]].

At the end of the [[2003 NFL season|2003 season]], Walter wasn't re-signed by the Patriots. Walter struggled at the tail end of that season, was cut for a week as he lost his job to [[Brooks Barnard]], then re-signed for the Patriots' final surge to their [[Super Bowl XXXVIII]] championship.

Walter's career appeared over, but he was signed by Seattle in November 2004 and punted in six regular season games and one playoff contest. Yet no team called in [[2005 in sports|2005]] and Walter, who underwent surgery on his left shoulder in October, filed his retirement papers with the league.

As Walter rehabilitated his shoulder injury, he was motivated by his [[physical therapist]] to make a comeback. He told the ''[[Boston Globe]]'' that he had been striking the ball as well as he ever has, and both the [[Houston Texans|Texans]] and [[Jacksonville Jaguars|Jaguars]] had him in for tryouts.

Walter was re-signed by the Patriots on November 22, 2006, after [[Josh Miller (punter)|Josh Miller]] was placed on [[injured reserve]]. However, Walter himself suffered a season-ending injury December 17 against the Houston Texans, and was placed on injured reserve two days later.

'''Kenneth Lee Stills Sr.''' (born September 6, 1963) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Safety (American football position)|safety]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Wisconsin Badgers football|Wisconsin Badgers]]. He is the father of [[American football]] [[wide receiver]] [[Kenny Stills]].

Stills was selected by the [[Green Bay Packers]] in the eighth round of the [[1985 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1985 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1985/draft.htm |access-date=2023-10-05 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He played [[college football]] at [[University of Wisconsin–Madison|Wisconsin]]. His first start in the NFL came against the [[Chicago Bears]], the Packers' most hated rivals during the 1980s, and he memorably cost his team a 15-yard penalty for shoving [[Matt Suhey]] at the line of scrimmage. Stills also played for the [[Minnesota Vikings]] for one season before retiring.

He was a former [[head coach]] for the [[River City Rage]] of the [[United Indoor Football]] and running backs coach for the [[Los Angeles Xtreme]] of the [[XFL (2001)|XFL]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=OU receiver Kenny Stills practices what he preaches |url=http://newsok.com/ou-receiver-kenny-stills-practices-what-he-preaches/article/3489556 |access-date=15 October 2014 |website=NewsOK.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.all-xfl.com/losangelesxtreme/community/personnel.shtml |title=Football Operations |publisher=all-xfl.com |access-date=15 October 2014}}</ref> He was also formerly the running backs coach at IMG Academy. Stills is currently the Head Football Coach at [[Bishop McLaughlin Catholic High School]] in [[Pasco County]], [[Florida]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://bishopmclaughlinathletics.com/2020/04/06/2020-varsity-football-message-head-football-ken-stills-sr/|title=2020 Varsity Football Message – Head Football Coach Ken Stills Sr.|date=6 April 2020|access-date=April 19, 2020|archive-date=October 19, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201019152519/https://bishopmclaughlinathletics.com/2020/04/06/2020-varsity-football-message-head-football-ken-stills-sr/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Like many former NFL players of the 1980s, Stills lives with the physical effects from playing in an era which emphasized defense and had far fewer limitations on tackling. Nearly twenty years after retiring from the NFL, he suffered five [[slipped disk]]s in his spine, causing his left hand to be permanently numb.<ref>{{cite news|title=Post-NFL pain has hit Kenny Stills hard|url=http://www.jsonline.com/sports/packers/post-nfl-pain-has-hit-kenny-stills-hard-b99357495z1-276875521.html|publisher=[[Milwaukee Journal Sentinel]]|date=September 23, 2014|first=Tyler|last=Dunne}}</ref>

Stills has four children from two marriages. His older son [[Kenny Stills|Kenny]] played collegiately for [[Oklahoma Sooners football|Oklahoma]], was selected by the [[New Orleans Saints]] in the [[2013 NFL draft]] and was last with the [[New Orleans Saints]] in September 2021.<ref name="e480">{{cite web | last=Sigler | first=John | title=Kenny Stills promoted from Saints practice squad for Week 3 vs. Patriots | website=Saints Wire|publisher=USA Today | date=2021-09-25 | url=https://saintswire.usatoday.com/2021/09/25/kenny-stills-promoted-from-saints-practice-squad-for-week-3-vs-patriots/ | access-date=2025-02-04}}</ref>

'''Ken Payne''' (October 6, 1950 – August 1, 2011)<ref>{{cite web |title=Ken Payne |url=https://www.nearmintcards.com/blog/tag/ken-payne/ |website=Nearmint's Vintage Football Card Blog |accessdate=10 November 2019}}</ref> was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[wide receiver]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He sprinted and played [[college football]] at [[Langston University|Langston]], helping the team to an 11-0 record and the 1973 NAIA playoffs.<ref>{{cite web |title=Obituary for Kenneth Eugene Payne, Jr. at Pollard Funeral Home - Oklahoma City |url=https://www.pollardfuneralhome.net/obituary/6321857 |website=www.pollardfuneralhome.net |accessdate=10 November 2019 |language=en}}</ref> He was the fourth player drafted from the small college when the [[Green Bay Packers]] selected him in the sixth round of the [[1974 NFL draft]].
